Add the two equations: 2x = ${s + df}

2 books and 3 pencils cost ${Rp(T1 * 1000)}, while 1 book and 2 pencils cost ${Rp(T2 * 1000)}. What is the price of one book?
Let book = b and pencil = p (in thousands). 2b + 3p = ${T1} and b + 2p = ${T2}.
Multiply the second equation by 2: 2b + 4p = ${2 * T2}
Subtract: (2b + 4p) ${MINUS} (2b + 3p) = ${2 * T2} ${MINUS} ${T1} → p = ${p}
Elimination: make the coefficients of one variable equal, then subtract so that variable disappears.

A ${it} costs ${Rp(price)} and has a ${p}% discount. How much must be paid?
Discount = ${p}% × ${N(price)} = ${N(dc)}
Price to pay = ${N(price)} ${MINUS} ${N(dc)} = ${Rp(price - dc)}
Quick way: pay ${100 - p}% of the original price, i.e. ${N(price)} × ${(100 - p) / 100}.
A ${it} costs ${Rp(price)}. The shop gives a ${p1}% discount, then an extra ${p2}% off the price after the first discount. What is the final price?
Second discount ${p2}% of the new price: ${N(price * (100 - p1) / 100)} × ${(100 - p2) / 100} = ${Rp(final)}
A stacked discount of ${p1}% + ${p2}% is not ${p1 + p2}%! The second discount is taken from the already reduced price.
The price of an item rises from ${Rp(b)} to ${Rp(nw)}. By what percent did the price increase?
Increase = ${N(nw)} ${MINUS} ${N(b)} = ${N(nw - b)}
Percentage relative to the original price: ${N(nw - b)} ÷ ${N(b)} × 100% = ${p}%
Percent increase/decrease is always computed relative to the original value.
After a ${p}% discount, the price of a shirt becomes ${Rp(fin)}. What was the price before the discount?
Price after discount = ${100 - p}% of the original price.
${100 - p}% × original price = ${N(fin)}
original price = ${N(fin)} ÷ ${(100 - p) / 100} = ${Rp(base)}
Trap: adding ${p}% to the final price is wrong, because the ${p}% was taken from the original price.
A cake recipe for ${pp} people needs ${eg} eggs. How many eggs are needed for ${people} people?
For 1 person: ${eg} ÷ ${pp} = ${N(eg / pp)} eggs
For ${people} people: ${N(eg / pp)} × ${people} = ${need} eggs
Direct proportion: when one quantity goes up, the other goes up in the same ratio.
On a map with a scale of 1 : ${N(k)}, the distance between two cities is ${c} cm. What is the real distance (in km)?
Real distance = ${c} × ${N(k)} = ${N(c * k)} cm
From cm to km: divide by 100,000 (the same as removing 5 zeros).
${w1} workers can finish a project in ${days} days. How many days are needed if there are ${w2} workers (same speed)?
Total work = ${w1} × ${days} = ${w1 * days} (worker-days)
With ${w2} workers: ${w1 * days} ÷ ${w2} = ${nd} days
Inverse proportion: more workers means less time.
What is the length of the hypotenuse of the right triangle below?
Pythagoras: hypotenuse² = ${A}² + ${B}²
Hypotenuse = √${A * A + B * B} = ${C} cm
Common Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, and their multiples.
What is the length of the side marked with a question mark?
The hypotenuse (${C}) is the longest side.
Leg² = ${C}² ${MINUS} ${h ? A : B}² = ${C * C} ${MINUS} ${(h ? A : B) ** 2} = ${C * C - (h ? A : B) ** 2}
Length = √${C * C - (h ? A : B) ** 2} = ${h ? B : A} cm
If the unknown is not the hypotenuse, subtract. If it is the hypotenuse, add.
The two legs of a right triangle are ${a} cm and ${b} cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse (in simplest radical form)?
Hypotenuse² = ${a}² + ${b}² = ${s}
Hypotenuse = √${s}
Simplify: ${sqrtForm(s)} cm
After taking the root, simplify by looking for a perfect-square factor: √50 = √(25×2) = 5√2.
A ${C} m ladder leans against a wall. The foot of the ladder is ${A} m from the wall. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
The ladder, the ground and the wall form a right triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse.
Height² = ${C}² ${MINUS} ${A}² = ${C * C - A * A}
Height = √${C * C - A * A} = ${B} m
Always sketch the story first. Decide which side is the hypotenuse (the one opposite the right angle).
A rectangular field measures ${A} m × ${B} m. What is the length of the field's diagonal?
The diagonal splits the rectangle into two right triangles.
Diagonal² = ${A}² + ${B}² = ${A * A + B * B}
Diagonal = ${C} m
Cutting across is shorter than going around the edges: ${C} m vs ${A + B} m.
From home, Budi walks ${A} km north, then ${B} km east. How far is Budi in a straight line from home?
North and east are perpendicular directions.
Distance² = ${A}² + ${B}² = ${A * A + B * B}
Distance = ${C} km
Two perpendicular directions always form a right angle.

A bicycle wheel has a diameter of ${dia} cm (π = ${fr(22, 7)}). How many full turns does it make to travel ${N(dist)} m?
Wheel circumference = π × d = ${fr(22, 7)} × ${dia} = ${C} cm
Distance = ${N(dist)} m = ${N(C * n)} cm
Number of turns = ${N(C * n)} ÷ ${C} = ${n}
One turn of the wheel = one circumference. Make the units the same (cm or m) before dividing.
The diagram shows the math test scores of five students. What is the mean score?
Add all the values: ${data.join(' + ')} = ${sum}
Divide by the number of values: ${sum} ÷ 5 = ${m}
Mean = sum of all data ÷ number of data.

Median = ${med}

The mean of Rani's ${n} test scores is ${m}. What must her next score be so that the mean becomes ${t}?
Sum of the first ${n} scores = ${n} × ${m} = ${n * m}
Sum needed for ${n + 1} scores = ${n + 1} × ${t} = ${(n + 1) * t}
Next score = ${(n + 1) * t} ${MINUS} ${n * m} = ${x}
Use the total sum, not the mean: mean × number of data = sum of the data.
